analysis.one_liner: Raises penalties on insurers that violate surprise-billing protections or pay providers late.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the final two weeks of the 118th Congress, the bill was referred to the Senate health committee and died there without a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The No Surprises Act already bars most surprise medical bills and requires insurers to pay out-of-network providers what an arbitration process sets. This bill would give that law teeth: it raises the fine on insurers and employer health plans that violate the no-surprise-billing rules from $100 per failure to $10,000 per failure, adds a triple-difference penalty plus interest when plans pay providers late or not at all after arbitration, and requires twice-yearly reports to Congress on audits, complaints, and fines.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients protected by the No Surprises Act, whose rights would be enforced with real penalties instead of a nominal $100 fine, and out-of-network providers and hospitals who would be paid promptly after arbitration, with a triple-payment penalty if they are not.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the civil penalty on group health plans and insurers for violating core no-surprise-billing requirements from $100 per failure to $10,000 per failure under the public health, employer benefits (ERISA), and tax-code provisions of the law.

Adds a penalty for late payment or non-payment after an arbitration (independent dispute resolution) decision: the plan must pay the provider three times the gap between its initial payment and the determined out-of-network rate, plus interest, and must notify the Secretary when it pays.

Requires the Secretaries of Health and Human Services, Labor, and Treasury to report to Congress every six months on audits conducted, complaints filed by providers and enrollees, enforcement actions, total fines issued, and the most common violations.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers who sponsor group health plans would bear the higher penalty exposure and the triple-payment late penalty, costs that could partly flow into premiums or benefit costs.

drawbacks.text: Higher fines on insurers and employer plans are ultimately business costs, and some share could show up in premiums or employee benefit costs rather than being absorbed by company profits.

The triple-payment late penalty pays out-of-network providers, including hospitals and air ambulance operators, three times the shortfall — a substantial transfer toward a well-organized provider industry, not only a patient protection.
The bill raises penalties and reporting but does not simplify the underlying surprise-billing or arbitration rules, so disputes and compliance burdens on plans remain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: patients get a no-surprises law that is actually enforced, and insurers get real financial consequences for ignoring it. The main caveat is that plan penalties can leak into premiums, and the treble payment provision is a rich remedy that primarily benefits providers. On balance, the design targets compliance failures rather than rewriting the law, so the patient-side benefit likely outweighs the cost-shifting risk.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 16, 2024, about two weeks before the 118th Congress ended, was read twice and sent to the Senate health committee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress expired.

narrative.text: Senator Roger Marshall introduced the bill with Senator Michael Bennet as cosponsor on December 16, 2024, giving it one Republican and one Democratic sponsor.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day it was introduced; no further action appears in the record.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died in committee without a vote or a House companion moving.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer-sponsored health plans are better off, because they avoid the $10,000-per-violation fines and the triple-payment late penalty; patients gain nothing beyond the existing, weakly enforced rules.

for.name: Sen. Roger Marshall
for.role: U.S. Senator from Kansas, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to increase penalties for violations of the No Surprises Act's balance billing rules.

for.name: Sen. Michael Bennet
for.role: U.S. Senator from Colorado, original cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor at introduction, making the sponsorship bipartisan.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican senator sponsored the bill with one Democratic cosponsor, and no one spoke or voted against it on the record — it simply ran out of time, introduced two weeks before the Congress ended.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer-sponsored health plans
industries.note: The bill raises fines from $100 to $10,000 per violation of the no-surprise-billing rules and adds a triple-damage late-payment penalty after arbitration. These are direct costs to plans, which can partly pass them into premiums, though the penalties only trigger on noncompliance.

industries.industry: Out-of-network hospitals, physicians, and air ambulance operators
industries.note: Providers who win arbitration awards would be paid promptly, and late or non-paying plans would owe triple the shortfall plus interest. This strengthens payment enforcement but also channels money toward a well-resourced provider industry.

industries.industry: Patients with employer or marketplace coverage
industries.note: Patients are the intended beneficiaries: stronger fines and public reporting make the surprise-billing protections they rely on more than nominal.
